ssc.label: No SSC
ssc.definition: Dead start or paused. No elastic contribution; force comes from rate of development alone.

ssc.label: Slow SSC
ssc.definition: Contact > 250 ms, large joint displacement. Countermovement assists the jump.

ssc.label: Fast SSC
ssc.definition: Contact < 250 ms, small displacement. Trains tendon stiffness and reactive strength.

ssc.label: Eccentric only
ssc.definition: Deceleration and landing. No concentric phase to train.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

ssc.label: Not applicable

exercises.name: Pull-up
exercises.position: Closed chain, so the body moves to the bar and the trunk must resist swinging. Pronated grip puts the biceps at a mechanical disadvantage, which is what makes it harder than a chin-up and more lat-dominant.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, loadable. Hardest at the bottom from a dead hang.
cues: Start from a full dead hang
Lead with the elbows down and back
Chest to the bar, no kipping

exercises.name: Chin-up
exercises.position: Supination puts the biceps in its strongest line, so more load goes through the elbow flexors and most people manage more reps than a pull-up. Usually the kinder option for a shoulder, harsher for an elbow.
cues: Full hang, full range
Drive the elbows to the ribs
Control the lowering

exercises.name: Neutral Grip Pull-Up
exercises.position: Palms facing lets the shoulder sit in its most neutral rotation, which is why it is usually the best-tolerated of the three grips. Brachialis contributes more than in either other version.
cues: Shoulders down out of the ears at the start
Elbows straight down, not flared
Full range both ways

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown
exercises.position: Open chain, so the load is dialled rather than fixed at bodyweight — the standard way to train the pull-up pattern before a pull-up exists, and to overload it afterwards. The trunk does much less work than in a pull-up.
exercises.resistance: Cable, constant. Hardest near full stretch.
cues: Chest up, slight lean back and hold it
Pull to the collarbone, elbows down
Let the shoulder blades rise at the top

exercises.name: Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown
exercises.position: Neutral rotation at the shoulder with the load adjustable — the gentlest entry to vertical pulling, and the usual substitute when a pronated pulldown or pull-up bothers the shoulder.
cues: Pull to the upper chest
Elbows travel down the sides
Pause briefly at the bottom

exercises.name: Wide Grip Lat Pulldown
exercises.position: A wider grip shortens the elbow's range and moves the pull toward pure adduction in the frontal plane, so the arms contribute less. It also demands more shoulder external rotation, which not every shoulder has.
cues: Just wider than shoulders is enough
Elbows down, not back
Do not pull behind the neck

exercises.name: Bent Row
exercises.position: The back muscles are working while the spine holds a loaded hinge, so the erectors pay twice. Excellent for upper-back mass and a poor choice for a flexion-sensitive lower back — the reason supported rows exist.
cues: Hinge to about 45° and keep it there
Pull to the lower ribs
Stop the set when the torso starts rising

exercises.name: Pendlay Row
exercises.position: The bar resets on the floor every rep, so there is no eccentric to rebound from and the torso stays nearly horizontal. More concentric power, more lumbar demand than a standard bent row.
cues: Torso stays parallel to the floor
Full reset on the ground between reps
Explode the bar to the ribs

exercises.name: Single Arm Dumbbell Row
exercises.position: Supporting the torso on a bench removes the spinal load almost entirely, so the back can be trained heavily without a flexion demand. The default row for a lumbar-limited programme, and it allows more scapular range than a barbell.
cues: Let the shoulder blade reach forward at the bottom
Pull to the hip, not the shoulder
Keep the hips square to the floor

exercises.name: Chainsaw Row
exercises.position: Hand on a bench and feet staggered: less spinal load than a bent row, more trunk work than a fully supported row. The middle option when a bent row is too much for the back but a bench row feels too passive.
cues: Hips level — do not open toward the working side
Long range, drag the dumbbell back
Support arm takes weight, not all of it

exercises.name: Inverted Row
exercises.position: A horizontal pull with the spine unloaded and the trunk working as a plank, difficulty set by body angle rather than plates. The counterpart to the push-up and the cleanest bodyweight back exercise there is.
equipment: bar in a rack or low bar
cues: One line from heel to head
Chest to the bar, squeeze the blades
Raise the bar or bend the knees to make it easier

exercises.name: Ring Row
exercises.position: Rings let the hands rotate through the pull, so the shoulder picks its own path and the cuff works to control an unstable handle. Kinder to a sore shoulder than a fixed bar, harder to load precisely.
cues: Turn the palms up as you pull
Body straight, heels on the floor
Walk the feet forward to make it harder

exercises.name: Single Arm Ring Row
exercises.position: One arm doubles the load and adds a rotational demand the trunk must refuse. More an anti-rotation exercise with a rowing component than a pure back exercise.
cues: Shoulders stay square to the ceiling
Do not let the torso twist
Walk the feet back to regress

exercises.name: Low Cable Row
exercises.position: Seated and braced, with constant cable tension through a long scapular range. Most of the back work of a bent row with a fraction of the lumbar cost, which makes it a workhorse rather than a compromise.
exercises.resistance: Cable, constant. Hardest at full retraction.
cues: Let the arms reach forward fully at the start
Pull to the navel, elbows past the ribs
Torso nearly still — do not rock

exercises.name: Cable T-Bar Row
exercises.position: Standing and hinged like a bent row but with cable tension rather than a bar, so the resistance is constant and the load easier to dial. Still a loaded hinge, so the lumbar demand is real.
cues: Hinge and hold the torso angle
Drive the elbows past the ribs
Chest stays proud

exercises.name: Straight Arm Pulldown
exercises.position: Takes the elbow flexors out, so the lat is trained purely as a shoulder extensor. For a swimmer this is the closest gym movement to the catch and pull-through, and it is the way to load the lat when the biceps or elbow is the limiting factor in every other pull.
exercises.resistance: Cable, constant. Hardest with the arms forward.
cues: Small fixed bend at the elbow, keep it there
Sweep the arms down to the thighs
Hinge forward slightly and stay there

exercises.name: Rear Delt Fly
exercises.position: Horizontal abduction with the elbow nearly straight, which removes the lats and isolates the posterior delt and external rotators — the muscles that pressing volume tends to leave behind.
cues: Thumbs up, lead with the pinkies out
Very light — technique fails fast
Do not turn it into a row

exercises.name: Head Supported Rear Delt Row
stabilizers: deep trunk (low — head takes the load)
exercises.position: Resting the forehead on a support removes the isometric hinge, so the lower back does nothing and all the effort goes to the upper back. The rear-delt exercise to use when the back is the limiting factor.
equipment: bench or rack to rest on
cues: Let the head take your weight
Elbows wide, pull to the ribs
Pause at the top

exercises.name: Incline Bench Rear Delt Fly
stabilizers: minimal — the bench does the stabilizing
exercises.position: Chest on the bench removes every compensation including the hinge, so there is nowhere to cheat the weight up from. Strictest of the rear-delt variants and the lowest spinal cost.
cues: Chest stays on the pad
Arms sweep out, not back
Stop when you need momentum

exercises.name: Dumbbell Curl
exercises.position: The biceps long head crosses the shoulder, so shoulder position sets its length — standing with the arms at the side leaves it at moderate length, and taking the arms behind the body on an incline lengthens it. Another biarticular muscle where two 'biceps' exercises are not equivalent.
exercises.resistance: External. Hardest with the forearm horizontal.
cues: Elbows stay at the ribs
Supinate as you curl
Lower all the way

exercises.name: Hammer Curl
exercises.position: A neutral forearm takes the biceps out of its strongest line and shifts work to the brachialis and brachioradialis. Usually the better-tolerated curl for a sore elbow or wrist.
cues: Palms face each other throughout
No swinging
Full range

exercises.name: EZ Curl
exercises.position: The angled bar lets the wrists sit between pronation and supination, which most elbows and wrists prefer to a straight bar while still allowing both arms to be loaded together.
cues: Elbows pinned to the sides
Wrists neutral, not cocked back
Control the lowering

exercises.name: Zottman Curl
exercises.position: Curling supinated and lowering pronated trains the forearm extensors eccentrically in the same rep — one of very few exercises that loads the pronation–supination function directly. Useful for grip and elbow resilience rather than biceps size.
exercises.resistance: External. Eccentric is the hard part.
cues: Rotate at the top, not on the way up
Lower slowly with the palms down
Much lighter than a normal curl

swap_edges.same: Vertical pull, lat and teres major emphasis
swap_edges.changed: Bodyweight and closed chain, so the trunk works too

swap_edges.same: Horizontal pull for lats and mid-back
swap_edges.changed: One dumbbell and a bench instead of a loaded barbell

swap_edges.same: Horizontal pull through a long scapular range
swap_edges.changed: Bodyweight on rings; difficulty set by body angle
Isolated shoulder extension; no pulldown station needed

swap_edges.same: Horizontal pull, lats and rhomboids, lengthened bias
swap_edges.changed: Torso supported on a bench — the loaded hinge is gone
Seated and braced instead of holding a loaded hinge
Bodyweight with the spine unloaded; trunk works as a plank
Hand supported, so much less spinal demand
Chest supported — the isometric hinge is removed entirely
Seated rather than hinged
Neutral grip lets the shoulder sit in its least provocative rotation
Neutral grip and adjustable load
Removes the wide-grip external rotation demand
Elbow flexors removed — the lat works purely as a shoulder extensor
Neutral forearm, usually better tolerated by elbow and wrist
Dumbbells let each wrist find its own rotation
No elbow flexion under load at all
Load is dialled below bodyweight
Horizontal, and difficulty set by body angle
Both arms, so half the load and no anti-rotation demand
No machine — a bar in a rack, or rings
